claim: Scranton, Pennsylvania sold its municipal sewer system to a private utility. The Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission, the state's rate regulator, approved the transfer of the Scranton Sewer Authority's wastewater assets to Pennsylvania American Water on October 6, 2016 in a roughly $195 million deal covering about 31,000 customers in Scranton and Dunmore. The city banked about $83 million after debt was retired. In July 2024 the same commission approved the buyer's request for higher rates — 10.7 percent on water and 6.4 percent on wastewater — after the city had opposed a larger increase.

sources.label: Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission, "PUC Grants Conditional Approval for Sale of Scranton Sewer System to Pennsylvania-American Water Company" (October 6, 2016)
sources.quote: cost studies be presented by PAWC in its next rate case to ensure appropriate rate integration between the two systems

sources.label: City of Scranton, "PUC Approves PAWC Water Sewer Rate Increases" (July 11, 2024)

notes: The PUC release is the regulator's own; the rate-increase confirmation is the city's own release, which also records that the utility's original ask 'would have cost Scranton residents an estimated $220 more per year.' Deliberately does not assert a causal link between privatisation and the 2024 increase — the commission approved a statewide PAWC rate case, not a Scranton-specific one. The surfacing clip also says Scranton's electricity was privatised; Pennsylvania deregulated retail electricity statewide under Act 138 of 1996, which is not a municipal sale, so that claim is not recorded here.
